gloss: break, shatter; be broken; breaking, ruin; (also) grain, buy grain
summary: To break what was whole, so that it cannot be used or mended: a bone, a potter's vessel, a bow, a yoke, the tablets of the covenant, the pillars of idols; and in the passive a neck, a ship, a kingdom or a heart that is broken. The noun שֶׁבֶר is a fracture, and the breaking or ruin of a people, a wound that only Yahweh can heal; a broken heart is the sacrifice he does not despise, and his anointed is sent to bind it up (Isa 61:1; Luk 4:18). The same spelling names grain, שֶׁבֶר, and the verb “buy grain”, above all in Joseph's famine; how grain comes from “break” is not shown by the text or the cognates. Arabic ṯabara “destroy”, Ugaritic ṯbr, Aramaic and Syriac təḇar and Akkadian šebēru “break” show an older ṯ behind the ש.

words.gloss: break, break in pieces, shatter; be broken
words.summary: About 150 times. The qal breaks a thing (a bone, a vessel, a bow, an arm, a yoke, the staff of bread); the piel shatters, above all tablets, idols and pillars, trees and cedars, gates and bones; the niphal is to be broken, of things, of limbs, of kingdoms, and of the heart; the hiphil once brings a womb to the breaking open of birth (Isa 66:9), the hophal once is the prophet broken with his people (Jer 8:21). What is broken is past mending (Jer 19:11; Pro 29:1), unless Yahweh binds it up (Ezk 34:16; Psa 147:3).

stems.gloss: break, break in pieces; (participle passive) broken

senses.definition: To break a thing so that it is no longer whole: a bone, an earthen vessel, a jar, an arm, a bow, a staff.

evidence.note: Of the Passover lamb: “you shall not break a bone of it.” Quoted in Jhn 19:36.
The same law for the second Passover.
“So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel that cannot be made whole again.”
Jeremiah breaks the flask before the men's eyes.
An earthen vessel made unclean “you shall break”.
Gideon's three hundred “broke the jars”.
“Break the arm of the wicked.”
“I have broken the arm of Pharaoh … I will break his arms, the strong and the broken”: a broken arm cannot hold the sword.
“I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”
“Bow and sword and battle I will break from the land.”
“I will break the bow of Elam.”
“Yahweh has broken the staff of the wicked, the sceptre of rulers.”
“A bruised reed he will not break”: the servant's gentleness; quoted of Jesus in Mat 12:20.
“He will break it as the breaking of a potter's vessel, crushed without sparing.”
“A soft tongue breaks a bone.”
The lion “broke him and killed him”; and 1Ki 13:28 it had not broken the donkey.
“Reproach has broken my heart, and I am sick.”
“He heals the broken of heart (לִשְׁבוּרֵי לֵב) and binds up their wounds”: the passive participle.
שָׁבוּר, an animal with a broken limb, unfit for the altar, beside blind and maimed.
The men of Sodom came near “to break the door”.
Yahweh called an assembly against me “to crush my young men”.
“Those who eat his food will break him.”
“I broke upon it my boundary”: the limit cut for the sea.
“The wild donkeys break their thirst.”

senses.gloss: break a yoke, bonds; break power or pride
senses.definition: To break the yoke, bars or bonds by which a people is held in service, and so to set it free; or to break the strength or pride a people trusts in.

evidence.note: “I am Yahweh your God who brought you out of Egypt … I broke the bars of your yoke and made you walk upright.”
Hananiah: “I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.”
Hananiah breaks the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck; Yahweh answers, “you have broken yokes of wood, but you will make in their place yokes of iron.”
“In that day I will break his yoke from off your neck … and strangers shall no more make him serve.”
“They will be secure in their land, and know that I am Yahweh, when I have broken the bars of their yoke.”
“Now I will break his yoke from off you and burst your bonds.”
“To break Assyria in my land … and his yoke shall depart from them.”
“When I break there the yokes of Egypt.”
Israel itself: “long ago you broke your yoke and burst your bonds; you said, I will not serve.”
The great men “have broken the yoke, burst the bonds”.
“I will break the pride of your power.”
“I have broken Moab like a vessel no one wants.”
“I will break the bar of Damascus.”
“Break them with a double breaking (שִׁבָּרוֹן).”

senses.definition: To cut off the supply of bread on which life leans: to send famine.

evidence.note: “When I break your staff of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, and deliver it by weight.”
“I am breaking the staff of bread in Jerusalem; they shall eat bread by weight and with anxiety.”
“I break its staff of bread and send famine upon it.”
“He called a famine on the land; he broke every staff of bread”: the famine of Joseph's day.

stems.gloss: be broken; be broken in heart; be broken (of power, a kingdom)

senses.definition: Of a thing, a limb or an animal: to be broken, shattered or injured.

evidence.note: Eli fell backward, “and his neck was broken, and he died”.
“He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken.” With Exo 12:46, fulfilled at Jhn 19:36.
The earthen vessel the sin offering is boiled in “shall be broken”.
An animal in another's keeping “dies or is hurt (נִשְׁבַּר) or driven away”.
“The broken you have not bound up.”
“The broken I will bind up, and the sick I will strengthen.”
The worthless shepherd will not heal “the broken”.
Before “the pitcher is broken at the fountain”: the body failing in death.
“Broken cisterns that can hold no water.”
Jehoshaphat's ships “were broken” at Ezion-geber; 2Ch 20:37.
“The ship thought to be broken.”
Tyre the ship “broken by the seas”.
“The snare is broken, and we have escaped.”
“Their bows shall be broken”; Psa 37:17, “the arms of the wicked shall be broken.”
“Many shall stumble on it, and fall and be broken, and be snared and taken”; again Isa 28:13.
Its boughs, dried up, are broken off.
“The city of chaos is broken down.”
“Your incense altars shall be broken”; Ezk 6:6.
The boughs of the cedar, Assyria, broken in every channel.
“Let my arm be broken from its socket.”
“Unrighteousness shall be broken like a tree.”

senses.gloss: be broken in heart or spirit
senses.definition: Of the heart or spirit: to be crushed by grief or humbled before God; the broken in heart are those Yahweh is near to and heals.

evidence.note: “Yahweh is near to the broken of heart (לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב), and saves the crushed of spirit.”
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart, O God, you will not despise.”
“He has sent me to bind up the broken of heart.” Read by Jesus in Nazareth: “today this scripture has been fulfilled” (Luk 4:18, 21).
The Peshitta renders the phrase לִתְבִירַי לֵבָּא, the same root in Syriac.
“My heart is broken within me … because of Yahweh and his holy words.”

senses.gloss: be broken (of power, a kingdom, a man)
senses.definition: Of a kingdom, a horn, a city, or a man who hardens himself: to be broken in power, brought to ruin.

evidence.note: “He who is often reproved and hardens his neck will suddenly be broken, and there is no healing.”
“Suddenly he will be broken, and there is no healing.”
“When he was strong, the great horn was broken, and in its place came up four.” Explained in Dan 8:22.
“He shall be broken, but not by hand.”
“His kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven.”
“Moab is broken”; Jer 48:17, “How the strong staff is broken!”; Jer 48:25, “his arm is broken.”
“How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken!”
“Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken.”
“All your lovers are broken.”
“With a great breaking the virgin daughter of my people is broken.”
Tyre: “Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken.”
Egypt, a reed that broke when Israel leaned on it.
“When all her helpers are broken.”
“The rod that struck you is broken.”
“The uplifted arm is broken.”
The Cushites “were broken before Yahweh and before his army”.

senses.definition: To break a thing in many pieces or break it down: tablets, trees, cedars and rocks, gates and bars, bones and teeth, weapons, ships.

evidence.note: Seeing the calf, Moses “threw the tablets from his hands and shattered them beneath the mountain”.
“I shattered them before your eyes.”
“The first tablets, which you shattered”; Deu 10:2.
The hail “shattered every tree of the field”.
“The voice of Yahweh breaks the cedars; Yahweh shatters the cedars of Lebanon.”
A great wind “breaking the rocks before Yahweh”.
“He shattered the trees of their borders.”
“He has broken gates of bronze and cut bars of iron in two”; Isa 45:2.
“He has destroyed and broken her bars.”
“You have broken the teeth of the wicked.”
“I broke the jaws of the unrighteous.”
“He breaks the bow and cuts the spear in two.”
“With the east wind you shatter the ships of Tarshish.”
“You broke the heads of the sea monsters on the waters.”
Hezekiah: “like a lion he breaks all my bones”; Lam 3:4.
The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars of the house of Yahweh; Jer 52:17.
The goat “broke his two horns”.

senses.definition: To smash the pillars, altars and images of other gods, as the law commanded and the faithful kings did.

evidence.note: “You shall utterly overthrow them and shatter their pillars.”
“Break down their altars, shatter their pillars, cut down their Asherim, burn their images with fire.”
Hezekiah “shattered the pillars and cut down the Asherah”.
The people shattered the altars and images of Baal; 2Ch 23:17.
Josiah “shattered the pillars”.
“Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the images of her gods he has shattered to the ground.”
He will shatter the pillars of Beth-shemesh in Egypt.

stems.gloss: bring to the breaking open (of the womb)

senses.gloss: bring to the point of birth
senses.definition: To bring a womb to the breaking open of birth: once, of Yahweh bringing Zion's children to birth.

evidence.note: “Shall I bring to the breaking open (הַאֲנִי אַשְׁבִּיר) and not cause to bring forth? says Yahweh.” Zion bears a nation in one day (Isa 66:8).

senses.definition: Once, of the prophet broken with his people's breaking.

evidence.note: “For the breaking (שֶׁבֶר) of the daughter of my people I am broken (הָשְׁבָּרְתִּי); I mourn, dismay has taken hold of me.”

evidence.locator: Psa.34.21, נִשְׁבָּרָה → συντριβήσεται; Isa.42.3, יִשְׁבּוֹר → συντρίψει; Isa.61.1, נִשְׁבְּרֵי → συντετριμμένους; Psa.51.19; Psa.147.3; Lev.26.13; Jer.30.8; συντρίβω and its forms render שָׁבַר about 110 times

evidence.note: “These things happened that the scripture might be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken (συντριβήσεται)”: Exo 12:46; Num 9:12; Psa 34:21.
“To heal the broken (συντετριμμένους) of heart”, Isa 61:1, in the TR.
“As the vessels of a potter are broken (συντρίβεται)”, as Jer 19:11.
The fetters “broken in pieces (συντετρῖφθαι)”.
“A bruised reed he will not break (κατεάξει)”: Isa 42:3, יִשְׁבּוֹר, quoted of Jesus; the Septuagint has συντρίψει.
The soldiers broke (κατέαξαν) the legs of the other two, but not his, for he was dead already.

parallels.note: “Crush”: the bruised reed beside the breaking.
“Crushed”: the broken heart beside the crushed spirit or heart.
“Burst”: breaking the yoke beside bursting the bonds.
“Cut down”: the altars and Asherim beside the shattered pillars, the hammer of the earth.

opposites.note: “Bind up”: what is broken is bound up and healed by Yahweh and his shepherd.
“Heal”: the broken past healing, or healed by Yahweh.

phrases.gloss: break the staff of bread: send famine
break the yoke: set free from service

words.gloss: breaking, fracture; ruin, disaster; wound (of a people); (once) interpretation of a dream
words.summary: About forty-five times. A broken bone or limb, and then the breaking of a people or a city: the cry of “breaking upon breaking” as the land is laid waste, the wound of the daughter of my people that false prophets heal lightly and Yahweh alone heals. Once, in Jdg 7:15, it is the interpretation of a dream; how that comes from the root's sense is not clear. The tokens BDB's lists put under this key by spelling include the grain (Gen 42; Amo 8:5; Neh 10:32) and the name Sheber (1Ch 2:48), which are separate words here.

senses.definition: A broken bone or limb, a blemish that bars a priest from the altar, and an injury repaid in kind.

evidence.note: No descendant of Aaron who has “a broken foot or a broken hand” may approach.
“Fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth.”
A bulging wall “whose breaking comes suddenly”, broken like a potter's vessel with not a shard left.
“As far as the Shebarim”, a place of breaks (quarries or ravines) below Ai.

senses.definition: The breaking of a land, a city or a man: devastation and downfall, often beside שֹׁד “destruction”.

evidence.note: “Breaking upon breaking is proclaimed, for the whole land is laid waste.”
“I bring evil from the north, and a great breaking”; Jer 6:1.
“Destruction and breaking (שֹׁד וָשֶׁבֶר) are in their highways”: quoted in Rom 3:16 of all, Jew and Greek, under sin.
“Destruction and breaking shall no more be heard within your borders; you shall call your walls Salvation.”
“Devastation and breaking, famine and sword.”
“The breaking of rebels and sinners together.”
A cry of breaking over Moab; Jer 48:3, 5.
“A great breaking” over Babylon; Jer 51:54.
“A great crash from the hills.”
“Devastation and breaking.”
They drink wine “but are not grieved over the breaking of Joseph”.
“Before breaking, pride; before stumbling, a haughty spirit.”
“Before breaking the heart of a man is lifted up.”
“He who makes his door high seeks breaking.”
Perversity in the tongue is “a breaking in the spirit”.
“You shall wail for breaking of spirit.”
Before Leviathan the mighty are afraid; “because of the breakings” they lose themselves.

senses.gloss: wound, breaking (of a people), to be healed
senses.definition: The breaking of Yahweh's people seen as a wound to be bound up and healed, which false prophets heal lightly and Yahweh alone heals.

evidence.note: “They have healed the breaking of my people lightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there is no peace”; Jer 8:11.
“For the breaking of the daughter of my people I am broken.”
“Woe is me for my breaking; my wound is grievous.”
“Your breaking is incurable, your wound is grievous”; Jer 30:15; and then, “I will restore health to you and heal your wounds” (Jer 30:17).
“Over the breaking of the daughter of my people”; Lam 3:48; 4:10.
“Your breaking is great as the sea; who can heal you?”
“In the day Yahweh binds up the breaking of his people and heals the wound of his blow.”
“Heal its breaches, for it totters.”
Of Nineveh: “there is no easing of your breaking.”
“When I bring your breaking among the nations.”

senses.definition: Once: the explanation of a dream, what the dream “breaks open” to mean. The link to the root's sense is not clear.

evidence.note: “When Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation (שִׁבְרוֹ), he bowed down.”

evidence.locator: Isa.59.7, שֶׁבֶר → ταλαιπωρία (with σύντριμμα for שֹׁד)

evidence.note: “Destruction and misery are in their ways”: Isa 59:7, שֹׁד וָשֶׁבֶר.

evidence.locator: σύντριμμα renders שֶׁבֶר ×10, e.g. Jer.4.20; Lam.2.11

evidence.note: σύντριμμα in Paul's quotation of Isa 59:7.

words.summary: Nine times: the grain Jacob heard was in Egypt, which his sons bought and carried home in the famine, and the grain sold in the market (Amo 8:5; Neh 10:32). It is grain as food, bought and sold. Its tie to “break” is not shown: no verse and no cognate found so far uses this root for grain, and the root's cognates all mean break or destroy; the reading “broken, threshed grain” is a guess. Its kin is the verb שָׁבַר “buy grain”, formed from it.

senses.definition: Grain as food, stored, bought and sold, above all in time of famine.

evidence.note: “Jacob saw that there was grain (שֶׁבֶר) in Egypt.” Stephen: “Jacob heard there was grain (σῖτα) in Egypt” (Act 7:12).
“Carry grain for the famine of your households.”
They loaded their grain on their donkeys.
“When they had finished eating the grain they had brought from Egypt.”
Benjamin's sack, with “his grain money”.
Joseph gathered the silver “for the grain which they bought”.
“When will the new moon be over, that we may sell grain, and the sabbath, that we may open the wheat?”
“If the peoples of the land bring wares and any grain to sell on the sabbath, we will not buy.”
Stephen's telling of Gen 42:1–2.

evidence.locator: Gen.42.2; Gen.43.2; Gen.47.14, שֶׁבֶר → σῖτος; Gen.42.1 → πρᾶσις “sale”

evidence.note: “Jacob heard that there was grain (σῖτα) in Egypt”: Gen 42:1–2.

words.summary: About two dozen times, formed from the noun שֶׁבֶר “grain”: the qal buys food, mostly grain in Joseph's famine, the hiphil sells it. It shares the noun's unclear tie to “break”. BDB's lists put some tokens under both this key and the verb “break” by spelling: Gen 41:57; 42:3, 5 are “buy”, Gen 19:9; Isa 14:25; Lam 1:15 are “break”.

stems.gloss: buy grain, buy food; (once) sell grain

senses.definition: To buy grain or food with silver; in Isaiah, the call to “buy” what is given without price.

evidence.note: “Go down there and buy for us from there, that we may live and not die.”
Ten brothers went down “to buy grain from Egypt”.
“All the earth came to Egypt to Joseph to buy.”
“From the land of Canaan, to buy food (לִשְׁבָּר־אֹכֶל).”
“Go again, buy us a little food”; Gen 44:25.
“You shall buy food from them for silver, that you may eat; and you shall also buy (תִּכְרוּ) water from them for silver.”
“Come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without silver and without price.”
Joseph opened the storehouses “and sold (וַיִּשְׁבֹּר) to Egypt”: the qal once of the seller.

senses.definition: To sell grain or food, to let others buy it.

evidence.note: Joseph “was the one who sold (הַמַּשְׁבִּיר) to all the people of the land”.
“He who holds back grain, the people curse him; but blessing is on the head of him who sells.”
“You shall sell me food for silver.”
“That we may sell grain … making the ephah small.”
“And sell the refuse of the wheat.”
“I counsel you to buy (ἀγοράσαι) from me gold refined by fire”: the call of Isa 55:1 to buy what money cannot.

words.summary: Five times, always plural: the breakers of the sea, beside גַּלִּים “waves”; in the psalms and in Jonah, the overwhelming of one under God's hand, and “the breakers of death”. The wave that breaks on the shore.

senses.definition: The breaking waves of the sea, used of overwhelming distress and of death.

evidence.note: “You cast me into the deep … all your breakers and your waves (גַּלֶּיךָ) passed over me.”
“Deep calls to deep at the sound of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me.”
“You have afflicted me with all your breakers.”
“Mightier than the breakers of the sea, Yahweh on high is mighty.”
“The breakers of death surrounded me.”

words.gloss: place of breaking open: the mouth of the womb
words.summary: Three times: the opening of the womb, where the child breaks forth at birth. “Children have come to the opening, and there is no strength to bring forth” was Hezekiah's picture of Jerusalem's helplessness before Assyria.

senses.gloss: mouth of the womb, the point of birth
senses.definition: The opening of the womb through which a child is born; to come to it is to reach the moment of birth.

evidence.note: “Children have come to the opening (מַשְׁבֵּר), and there is no strength to bring forth”; Isa 37:3.
“The pains of a woman in labour come on him; he is an unwise son, for at the time he does not stand in the opening of children.”
“Sudden destruction comes on them, as birth pain (ὠδίν) on a woman with child.”

words.summary: Twice: a breaking, of enemies and of the loins in grief.

senses.definition: A breaking: ruin brought on enemies, or the breaking of the body in grief.

evidence.note: “Bring on them the day of evil, and break them with a double breaking.”
“Groan with breaking of loins and with bitterness.”

words.summary: Scripture's Aramaic form of the root, with ת for the older ṯ where Hebrew has ש: once, in Daniel's interpretation of the image.

senses.definition: Easily broken: the part of the last kingdom that is like clay.

evidence.note: “As the toes of the feet were part iron and part clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong (תַקִּיפָה) and partly brittle (תְבִירָה).”

words.summary: The Peshitta's verb for “break”, in the very passages where the New Testament takes up the Hebrew שָׁבַר: the reed not broken (Isa 42:3), the broken of heart (Isa 61:1), the bone not broken (Exo 12:46).

senses.definition: To break a thing; the passive participle תְּבִירָא, broken.

evidence.note: “A bruised reed he will not break (נֶתְבַּר)”, Isa 42:3.
“To heal the broken of heart (לִתְבִירַי לֵבָּא)” from Isa 61:1, and “to set the broken (לִתְבִירֵא) at liberty” from Isa 58:6.

senses.definition: To break in pieces, to break limbs.

evidence.note: The soldiers “broke (תַבַּרוּ) the legs” of the first and of the other.
The Jews asked Pilate that their legs be broken.
“Seeing he was dead already, they did not break his legs.”
The fetters he had shattered (מְתַבַּר).

senses.definition: To be broken.

evidence.note: “That the scripture might be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken (נֶתְּתְבַּר)”: Exo 12:46; Psa 34:21.

cognates.gloss: (God) destroyed him with a destruction from which he does not rise again; perish; (ṯubūr) perdition, destruction; also restrain, hold back
cognates.note: Arabic keeps the destructive end of the root, the ruin of the broken (the niphal's kingdoms broken, the noun's “breaking” of a land), not the plain breaking of a thing. It shows ṯ behind ש. Arabic تَبَّرَ “break in pieces, destroy” has t, not ṯ, and is taken by Wiktionary as a loan from Aramaic (تِبْر “broken gold”), so it is not recorded as a cognate.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 330, art. ثبر, ثَبَرَهُ (n4321)
evidence.note: “He (God) destroyed him with a destruction from which he should not rise again … He perished.” Also “He confined him; or restrained … him.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 330, art. ثبر, ثُبُورٌ (n4325)
evidence.note: “Perdition … destruction from which there is no rising again” (Kur xxv. 14).

cognates.gloss: break, smash, be broken; (šebru) broken, broken piece
cognates.note: The same plain sense as the Hebrew verb, and an adjective and noun “broken; a broken piece” as שֶׁבֶר “fracture”. Akkadian š stands for both older š and ṯ, so it does not show which.

evidence.locator: armep x000039790, šebēru [break] V (meanings “be broken”, “break”, “break up”, “smash”)
armep x000018500, šebru [broken] AJ (“broken; broken piece”)

cognates.note: Ugaritic keeps ṯ apart from š, and writes this root with ṯ.

cognates.gloss: break; (passive participle) broken; (taḇrā) break, fracture, breach, misfortune
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic of the Targums: the Targum renders the Hebrew שָׁבַר by תְּבַר (Gen 19:9; Jer 19:10) and שֶׁבֶר “fracture” by תַּבְרָא (Lev 24:20; 21:19). Aramaic t answers to older ṯ.

evidence.locator: s.v. תְּבַר, citing Targ. Gen. XIX, 9; Targ. Jer. XIX, 10; part. pass. תְּבִיר, Targ. Ps. XXXI, 13; Targ. Jer. II, 13
s.v. תַּבְרָא, תְּבָרָא, “break, fracture; breach, misfortune”, citing Targ. Lev. XXIV, 20; Targ. O. Lev. XXI, 19; Targ. Job VI, 21

cognates.note: The Syriac of the Peshitta, used where the New Testament quotes the Hebrew verses (Mat 12:20; Luk 4:18; Jhn 19:36); those uses are recorded as the entry's Syriac word.
Ge'ez s stands for older s, š and ṯ alike, so it does not show which.

doctrine.statement: The law of the Passover lamb says, “you shall not break a bone of it” (Exo 12:46; Num 9:12), and the psalm says of the righteous man, “many are the evils of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all; he keeps all his bones, not one of them is broken” (Psa 34:20–21). At the cross the soldiers broke the legs of the two crucified with Jesus, “but when they came to Jesus and saw that he was dead already, they did not break his legs … for these things happened that the scripture might be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken” (Jhn 19:32–36). Paul writes, “Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us” (1Co 5:7). From the verses: Jesus died truly, before the soldiers came to him, as the Passover lamb whose bones the law kept whole, and as the righteous man whom Yahweh delivered out of all his troubles, raising him from the dead.

“Yahweh is near to the broken of heart, and saves the crushed of spirit” (Psa 34:19); “the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psa 51:19), said by David after his sin, when he knew that God did not delight in sacrifice alone (Psa 51:18). The opposite is pride: “before breaking, pride, and before stumbling, a haughty spirit” (Pro 16:18). Yahweh “heals the broken of heart and binds up their wounds” (Psa 147:3), and the anointed one of Isa 61:1 is sent “to bind up the broken of heart”; Jesus read that passage in the synagogue at Nazareth and said, “today this scripture has been fulfilled in your ears” (Luk 4:18–21), and Peter says “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with holy spirit and with power” (Act 10:38). Of the same servant it is written, “a bruised reed he will not break” (Isa 42:3; Mat 12:20). From the verses: God accepts the man whose pride is broken, not the one who trusts in himself, and he heals him through Jesus, the man he anointed with his spirit to do it.

Yahweh's first act for Israel is told in this word: “I am Yahweh your God who brought you out of Egypt … I broke the bars of your yoke and made you walk upright” (Lev 26:13). If they would not listen, he would “break the pride of your power” and “break your staff of bread” (Lev 26:19, 26), and yet then “remember my covenant with Abraham, and remember the land” (Lev 26:42). Hananiah broke the yoke from Jeremiah's neck and promised its breaking within two years, and was answered, “you have broken yokes of wood, but you will make yokes of iron” (Jer 28:10–13). The breaking is promised for another day: “in that day I will break his yoke from off your neck … and they shall serve Yahweh their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them” (Jer 30:8–9); “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David … and they shall be secure in their land, and know that I am Yahweh, when I have broken the bars of their yoke” (Ezk 34:23–27). The angel told Mary of her son, “the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever” (Luk 1:32–33). From the verses: as Yahweh broke Israel's yoke in Egypt, he will break it again when he raises up David's son to reign, and Israel will dwell securely in the land promised to Abraham; a breaking of the yoke announced before Yahweh's time is false prophecy.

Open questions: (1) grain and “buy grain”: no cognate found ties grain to this root; the root's ṯbr cognates all mean break or destroy and so count against both words; “broken, threshed grain” or “rations broken off” are guesses. Leads not followed: Ugaritic or South Arabian for grain; Old Aramaic. (2) Jdg 7:15 שִׁבְרוֹ “its interpretation”: the link to break is not clear; Akkadian šabrû “interpreter of dreams” (Oracc armep x000077740) is usually taken from barû “see”, not this root, and is not recorded. (3) Gen 41:56 וַיִּשְׁבֹּר is a qal with the sense “sell”; the corpus has no hiphil there. (4) Leads not checked in their own dictionaries: Ugaritic ṯbr in DULAT, Ge'ez sabara in Leslau or Dillmann, Punic šbr in Krahmalkov (each cited here only through the Proto-Semitic list and Wiktionary).
